name: Task 1 Data Language
summary: Rose by/to, the number/amount of, and describing figures.

paragraphs: Task 1 asks you to report data accurately: numbers, trends and comparisons. This uses a special set of language that you will see in almost every report: rose to and rose by, the number of and the amount of, peaked at, a third of, between… and. Small slips in these phrases can change the meaning of the data, which makes them more serious than they look.

This unit brings together the grammar of describing figures. Some of it repeats points from earlier units, such as prepositions and word forms, but here everything is focused on one goal: writing a clear, accurate Task 1 report.

blocks.title: The rule in one line
blocks.text: Describe data precisely: the right noun (number / amount), the right preposition (to / by / of / in) and the right form (rose sharply / a sharp rise).

paragraphs: Task Achievement in Task 1 depends on reporting the data accurately. If you write rose to 20% when you mean rose by 20%, the examiner sees a factual error, not just a grammar slip.
Data language also makes up a large part of your Task 1 grammar and vocabulary. Using it correctly, and with some variety, is one of the clearest ways to show control of academic English.

sections.title: Rule 1: Verbs and nouns for trends
sections.label: Rule 1: Verbs and nouns for trends

paragraphs: Most Task 1 sentences describe a trend: something went up, went down or stayed the same. English has a verb and a noun for most trends, which lets you vary your sentences.
Use the past simple for verbs when the data is in the past, and remember the irregular forms: rise → rose → risen, fall → fell → fallen, grow → grew → grown.

rows: a fall, a decrease, a decline, a drop
remained stable, stayed the same, leveled off
peaked at, reached a peak of
hit a low of, fell to a low of

sections.title: Rule 2: To, by, from, at, of and in
sections.label: Rule 2: To, by, from, at, of and in

paragraphs: Each small preposition in Task 1 has a precise meaning. To gives the new figure, by gives the size of the change, from gives the starting figure, and at gives the figure at one point.
After a noun, use of for the size of the change (a rise of 5%) and in for what changed (a rise in prices).

rows: size of the change (after a noun)
There was a rise in sales.

items.text: There was an increase of house prices.
There was an increase in house prices.
It reached a peak of $3.50. / It peaked at $3.50.

sections.title: Rule 3: Number, amount, proportion or percentage?
sections.label: Rule 3: Number, amount, proportion or percentage?

paragraphs: The noun you choose must match the data. The number of is for countable things (people, cars), the amount of is for uncountable things (money, water), and the proportion of or the percentage of is for parts of a whole.
Also note: percentage is a noun, while percent (or %) follows a number. You write the percentage of students, but 40 percent of students.

sections.title: Rule 4: Rose sharply or a sharp rise
sections.label: Rule 4: Rose sharply or a sharp rise

paragraphs: There are two main ways to describe how much something changed. You can use a verb with an adverb (rose sharply) or an adjective with a noun (a sharp rise). Both are correct, and using both gives your report variety.
The mistake is mixing the two: rose sharp or a sharply rise.
Time phrases tell the reader exactly when each change happened. The most common error is mixing the pairs: between always goes with and, and from always goes with to.
Use by + year when you mean “at or before that time”. With past data, it is often followed by the past perfect: By 2020, sales had doubled.

rows: over the period / during the decade
It remained the highest throughout the period.

paragraphs: Task 1 also asks you to make comparisons. Use comparative forms correctly (higher than, twice as high as) and make sure you compare like with like.
Multiples are useful but easy to get wrong. The pattern is twice / three times as + adjective + as, or twice / three times + the + noun + of.

rows: Sales in A were higher than those in B.
A's figure was twice as high as B's.
A had three times the number of visitors.
The figure was similar to that in 2010.

paragraphs: You do not always need exact figures. Approximate language such as about, around, just over and nearly sounds natural and is useful when the data is not precise. Fractions such as a quarter and a third are also good alternatives to percentages.
Remember that a fraction needs of before a noun phrase: a third of the students, not a third the students.
Every Task 1 report needs an overview: a short summary of the main trends or features. It usually starts with Overall or In general, followed by the most important patterns, without detailed numbers.
Use the past simple for past data and keep the overview general. Phrases such as the most noticeable feature and the main trend help you write it clearly.

items.text: Overall, sales of coffee rose, while tea sales fell.
In general, City A had the highest figures throughout the period.
The most noticeable feature is the sharp rise in online shopping.

paragraphs: Here is how accurate data language looks in a real Task 1 report.

rows: Sales rose by 15%, from 400 to 460 units.
There was a sharp increase in the number of visitors.
adjective + noun; increase in; number of
Country A's figure was twice as high as Country B's.
Just over half of the budget was spent on housing.

paragraphs: These five errors are among the most common data language mistakes in Task 1 reports.
Use this routine on every sentence that contains a figure.

steps: Check every figure: is it the new figure (to), the size of the change (by) or the starting figure (from)?
Check the noun: number (countable), amount (uncountable), proportion / percentage (parts of a whole).
Check the form: rose sharply or a sharp rise, never rose sharp.

furtherStudy.title: IDP IELTS: Key Language for Reporting Figures and Trends

cards.why: The change was 10%, so we use by. To would mean the new price was 10%.

cards.front: Unemployment fell ____ 5% in 2020, its lowest level.
cards.why: 5% is the new figure, so we use to.

cards.front: There was a sharp increase ____ the number of tourists.
cards.why: After increase, in shows what changed.

cards.front: The ____ of money spent on food fell.
cards.why: Money is uncountable, so we use the amount of.

cards.front: Sales rose ____ in the second half of the year.
cards.why: Rose is a verb, so it needs an adverb.

cards.front: The data covers the years between 2000 ____ 2020.
Forty ____ of households had a car.
cards.why: After a number, we use percent. Percentage is used without a number: the percentage of households.

cards.front: City A's figure was twice as high ____ City B's.
cards.why: The multiple pattern is twice as + adjective + as.
Peaked at gives the highest figure. Reached is followed directly by the figure, with no at.

cards.front: By 2020, the number of users ____ doubled.
cards.why: By + a past year shows the change was complete before that time, so we use the past perfect.

errors.hint: What word does between always pair with?
errors.explanation: Between pairs with and; from pairs with to (Rule 5).

errors.hint: After the noun peak, which preposition gives the figure?
errors.explanation: Reached a peak of / peaked at (Rule 2).

blanks.hint: first letter: r or i or c · meaning: became higher
first letter: s or m · meaning: by a small amount

errors.hint: Percent or percentage after a number?
errors.explanation: After a number, use percent (Rule 3).

errors.hint: Does lower need more?
errors.explanation: Lower is already comparative; do not add more (Rule 6).

blanks.hint: first letter: i or r or g · meaning: became higher
first letter: l or b or g · meaning: most significant in size

errors.hint: Is coal's share being compared with all the others?
errors.explanation: Use the superlative for the biggest of a group (Rule 6).

errors.hint: Is 30% the new figure or the size of the change?
errors.explanation: From… to gives the start and end figures (Rule 2).

blanks.hint: first letter: f or d · meaning: become lower
first letter: r or b · meaning: what is left

errors.hint: Which form describes the verb increased?
errors.explanation: Verbs are described by adverbs (Rule 4).

errors.hint: Is 4% the new figure or the size of the change?
errors.explanation: To gives the new figure; by gives the change (Rule 2).

blanks.hint: verb (past simple) · meaning: did not go up or down
adjective (comparative) · meaning: less high

errors.hint: Can tourists be counted?
errors.explanation: Use the number of with countable nouns (Rule 3).

errors.hint: What is the pattern for multiples?
errors.explanation: Use twice as + adjective + as (Rule 6).

errors.hint: After increase, which preposition shows what changed?
errors.explanation: In shows what changed; of gives the size (Rule 2).

blanks.hint: adjective · meaning: great in size and easy to see
adjective · meaning: almost unchanged

errors.hint: What word completes the pattern as much…?
errors.explanation: The pattern is as much as, never as much than (Rule 6).

errors.hint: Which preposition goes with a month?
errors.explanation: Months take in (Rule 5).

blanks.hint: verb (past simple) · meaning: reached its highest point
verb (past participle) · meaning: shared out
adjective · meaning: changing with the time of year

errors.hint: Which verb form follows to?
errors.explanation: After to, use the base form: to rise, not to rose (Word Form, Rule 7). Rise → rose → risen (Tenses, Rule 9).

errors.hint: Is City Z compared with one city or with all of them?
errors.explanation: Use the superlative for the smallest of a group (Rule 6).

errors.hint: Which preposition always follows similar?
errors.explanation: Similar always takes to (Rule 6).

blanks.hint: adverb · meaning: at a fast speed
verb · meaning: get to

errors.hint: From 30%… to or by 38%?
errors.explanation: From pairs with to for the end figure (Rule 2).

errors.hint: Does percent take -s after a number?
errors.explanation: After a number, percent has no -s (Rule 3).

errors.hint: Review (Subject–Verb Agreement): what is the head noun?
errors.explanation: The head noun is change, which is singular (Subject–Verb Agreement, Rule 1).

blanks.hint: meaning: by a large amount
meaning: became higher

errors.hint: Review (Articles): website is countable and singular.
errors.explanation: A singular countable noun cannot stand alone (Articles, Rule 1).

errors.hint: Which form describes the verb rose?
errors.explanation: Verbs are described by adverbs (Rule 4).

fixes: three times as high as on Monday
three times as high as those on Monday
three times as high as Monday's
errors.hint: What is the pattern for multiples, and what is being compared?
errors.explanation: Use three times as + adjective + as, and compare visits with visits (Rule 6).

blanks.hint: meaning: suddenly and by a large amount
meaning: reaching its final level

errors.hint: Can buildings be counted?
errors.explanation: Use the number of with countable nouns such as buildings (Rule 3).

blanks.hint: meaning: got rid of
meaning: newly put in
